title: The Donauradweg, Passau to Vienna Through the Wachau
subRegion: Danube Valley, Upper and Lower Austria

bestPeriod.note: July and August fill the riverside hotels and the ferries; late September gives you the Wachau grape harvest and empty cycle path.

summary: Seven days downstream from Passau to Vienna on Europe's most-ridden river path, with hand-pulled ferries and the Wachau terraces at the centre.
hook: The Danube does the work. You lose about 130 metres of altitude between Passau and Vienna and almost none of it feels like effort, which is why this route carries more cyclists than any other in Europe. The trick is to ride it in a way that is not a conveyor belt: cross by ferry whenever you can, sleep on the quiet bank, and give the Wachau two days instead of one.

snapshot.Base(s): Point-to-point: Passau → Schlögen → Linz → Grein → Melk → Krems → Vienna
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: 330-370 km, roughly 1,100 m cumulative gain; ~95% asphalt, short crushed-limestone sections in the Strudengau and on the Wachau south bank
snapshot.Getting There: Fly to Vienna (VIE), CAT or S7 to Wien Mitte, then ÖBB westbound to Passau Hbf (approx 3h30, one change at Linz). Return from Krems or Tulln on the Franz-Josefs-Bahn
snapshot.Who It Suits: First-time tourers, families with teenagers, anyone who wants distance without climbing

itinerary.title: Out of Passau on the Schlögen bend
itinerary.morning: Collect bikes in Passau. Donau Touristik of Linz and Eurobike Aktiv-Reisen both deliver hire bikes and e-bikes to Passau hotels and take them back in Vienna, a one-way rental here should never involve a return journey. Check rack bolts at the Dreiflüsseeck, where the Inn, Ilz and Danube meet.
itinerary.afternoon: Ride the German bank to Obernzell, cross into Austria near Jochenstein and pick up the Austrian Donauradweg signage. This upper stretch is quiet, wooded and slightly damp underfoot in the shaded cuttings. At Engelhartszell, the Trappist abbey of Stift Engelszell brews Gregorius and Nivard on site; the shop closes mid-afternoon.
itinerary.evening: The Schlögener Schlinge is the Danube's 180-degree hairpin, best seen from the water rather than above it. The Rollfähre at Au-Schlögen is a cable ferry that swings across on the current; approx €3.50 with a bike. Eat trout at the riverside and watch the barges take the bend.
itinerary.dayStats: 52 km, +160 m, asphalt throughout, one cable ferry.

itinerary.title: Locks, orchards and the Linz waterfront
itinerary.morning: North bank to Aschach, then the wide farmed flats below Eferding. The Aschach power station is the first of the run-of-river dams you cross; cyclists use the marked service deck.
itinerary.afternoon: Take the Ottensheim ferry to the south bank for the last 12 km into Linz, quieter, and it drops you at the Ars Electronica Center rather than in industrial Urfahr. The Lentos art museum and the Höhenrausch roof walks are both a five-minute push from the cycle path.
itinerary.evening: Linz eats late and well. The Altstadt around Hofgasse and Hauptplatz has the Linzer Torte in every window; the version at Konditorei Jindrak is the one locals argue about.
itinerary.dayStats: 63 km, +180 m, asphalt, two dam crossings and one ferry.

itinerary.title: The Strudengau narrows
itinerary.morning: Leave Linz on the south bank through Enns, the oldest chartered town in Austria, then Mauthausen. The memorial at the former concentration camp is 3 km uphill from the river; free, two hours, and it changes the tone of the day.
itinerary.afternoon: From Ardagger the valley tightens into the Strudengau. This is the only stretch where the path leaves asphalt for compacted limestone for a few kilometres, and where a modest headwind actually bites because the hills funnel it.
itinerary.evening: Grein is a small yellow-and-white river town with the oldest surviving theatre in Austria, the Greiner Stadttheater of 1791, still in its converted granary.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km, +210 m, asphalt with ~4 km crushed limestone.

itinerary.title: Nibelungengau to the gates of the Wachau
itinerary.morning: Persenbeug, Ybbs and the twin bridge at Ybbs-Persenbeug. The Nibelungengau is orchard country; roadside honesty stalls sell Most, the dry pressed cider, by the litre.
itinerary.afternoon: The pilgrimage church of Maria Taferl sits 120 m above the north bank on a spur, a genuine climb by this route's standards, and the terrace view down the valley is the reason to do it. Descend to Marbach and cross to Melk.
itinerary.evening: Stift Melk's baroque library and marble hall are worth the approx €15 entry; the last admission is around 16:30 outside high summer, so if you arrive late, do it first thing on Day 5.
itinerary.dayStats: 60 km, +290 m including the Maria Taferl spur, asphalt.

itinerary.title: Wachau, both banks
itinerary.morning: The Wachau is 36 km of terraced Grüner Veltliner and Riesling between Melk and Krems, and it is UNESCO-listed for the terraces, not the castles. Ride the south bank first through Aggsbach and Rossatz, less traffic, better light before noon.
itinerary.afternoon: Cross at Spitz-Arnsdorf or Weißenkirchen-St. Lorenz (approx €3 with bike, roughly every 30 minutes in season) and climb the Ruine Aggstein spur or the path up to Burgruine Dürnstein, where Richard the Lionheart was held. The ruin is a 25-minute walk from the village; leave the bike locked in the church square rack.
itinerary.evening: Dürnstein at dusk, once the coach parties have gone, is a different town. Wachauer Marille, the protected apricot, turns up as schnapps, dumplings and jam in every second window.
itinerary.dayStats: 44 km, +330 m with the ruin walk, asphalt plus short cobbled village lanes.

itinerary.title: Krems, Göttweig and the Kremstal edge
itinerary.morning: A loop day with no luggage. From Krems-Stein, take the Mautern ferry and climb to Stift Göttweig, the Benedictine abbey on its hill above the Danube confluence, 240 m of gain in 6 km on a quiet asphalt road.
itinerary.afternoon: Drop north into the Kremstal and follow the vineyard lanes back through Rohrendorf and Gedersdorf. Loess terraces, cellar rows, almost no cars.
itinerary.evening: Krems has the Kunsthalle and a genuine student population, so kitchens run past 21:00. The Heuriger courtyards in Stein pour their own wine by the Viertel.
itinerary.dayStats: 55 km, +420 m, asphalt with a 2 km gravel vineyard track.

itinerary.title: Tullnerfeld and the run into Vienna
itinerary.morning: Krems to Tulln on the north bank, 40 km of dead-flat levee path through the Tullnerfeld. The never-used Zwentendorf nuclear plant still stands beside the path.
itinerary.afternoon: Two honest options. Ride on: Tulln to Vienna is another 42 km, entering via Klosterneuburg and the Donauinsel to the Reichsbrücke. Or stop at Tulln Stadt and take the REX on the Franz-Josefs-Bahn into Wien Franz-Josefs-Bahnhof in 35 minutes.
itinerary.evening: Drop the bike at the Vienna return point, then Schwedenplatz and a Schnitzel that overhangs the plate.
itinerary.dayStats: 40 km (or 82 km riding through), +120 m, asphalt.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Donauschlinge
accommodationStrategy.description: It sits directly on the hairpin at the Day 1 finish, with a locked bike room, an outdoor wash point and a drying room that matters more than you think in May. The restaurant terrace looks straight down the bend, and the ferry landing is 100 metres away, so you start Day 2 without a road transfer.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €95-150 per night for two, half board available

accommodationStrategy.name: Gasthof Sänger Blondel
accommodationStrategy.description: A long-running house behind the blue abbey tower, with a walled courtyard where bikes go under lock and the owner's own cellar list on the table. Staying inside Dürnstein rather than at a Krems chain is the difference between seeing the village at 07:00 and seeing it at 11:00 with 300 river-cruise passengers.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead; there are barely twenty rooms.
accommodationStrategy.priceNote: €120-170 per night for two with breakfast

accommodationStrategy.name: Steigenberger Hotel & Spa Krems
accommodationStrategy.description: The pragmatic Day 6 choice: underground garage with bike cages, a proper spa for a rest-day evening, and a five-minute roll to the Krems train station for a bail-out. Ask for a room on the vineyard side, not the road side.
accommodationStrategy.booking: six weeks ahead, longer during the September harvest weekends.

logistics.emergency: 112 across Europe; in Austria, 144 for ambulance and 133 for police. Water rescue on the Danube is coordinated through 112.
logistics.money: Small Heurigen, ferry operators and honesty stalls are cash-only; carry €40-60 in small notes. Cards work everywhere else.

other.label: Bikes on ÖBB
other.text: Regional trains (REX, S-Bahn, Cityjet) take bikes without reservation, buy a bike day ticket, approx €5-7 for all of Austria. Long-distance Railjet and Intercity services require a compulsory bike reservation, approx €3 on top of the bike ticket, and the slots for the Linz-Vienna corridor sell out on summer Sundays. Book them in the ÖBB app the moment your dates are fixed.

other.label: The Wachaubahn
other.text: between Krems and Emmersdorf runs seasonally with open bike wagons and is the standard fallback if the weather turns on Day 5.

other.label: Ferries
other.text: The Wachau and Schlögen crossings are private operations, cash-friendly, roughly €2.50-4.00 per person with a bike, and they stop when the Danube runs high. Check water levels on the Austrian hydrographic service before you rely on a specific crossing.

other.label: Luggage transfer
other.text: Donau Touristik, Eurobike Aktiv-Reisen and Austria Radreisen all move bags hotel-to-hotel on this corridor for roughly €12-18 per bag per day. Book it as a package with the bike hire, not separately.

other.label: Data
other.text: Austrian coverage along the river is uniformly good. EU roaming applies; the German first day is on the same terms.

other.label: Opening traps
other.text: Village bakeries shut by 12:00 on Saturday and stay shut Sunday. Abbey ticket offices close admissions 45-60 minutes early; Monday closes many small museums.

other.label: Legal
other.text: Helmets are compulsory in Austria only for under-12s. Cycling with a blood alcohol level above 0.8‰ is an offence and is enforced in the Wachau. Bike lights are legally required from dusk.

proTips: Ride the Wachau west-to-east, which is what this itinerary does, the prevailing wind runs downstream and the terraces face you rather than glare at you.
Book the ÖBB bike reservation for the Passau approach on a Friday train, not a Saturday one; the Saturday morning westbound Railjets are the ones that fill with cyclists heading upstream.
Cross to the south bank at Ottensheim rather than riding into Linz on the north. It cuts the industrial approach and lands you at the Ars Electronica Center.
In Dürnstein, walk to the ruin at 07:30. The gate is unstaffed, the path is empty and the light down the valley is the reason people photograph the Wachau.
On the Göttweig climb, go up the Furth side and come down the Palt side. The descent is smoother and the abbey terrace faces the morning sun.

packingNotes: Two pairs of padded shorts. Seven consecutive days on a saddle punishes a single pair.
A rain jacket that actually breathes, Danube valley showers are short, warm and heavy in June.
A cable lock long enough to pass through both wheels and a fixed rack; village churches and ruins have public racks but no supervision.
Two bottles minimum. Public drinking fountains are common in Upper Austria and scarce in the Tullnerfeld.
Spare tube, tyre levers, a multi-tool and a compact pump, even on a hire bike. The nearest shop can be 30 km away.
Cash in small denominations for ferries and Heurigen.
whatCouldGoWrong: **High water closes the ferries.** After heavy Alpine rain the Wachau crossings suspend service and stretches of the path near Grein flood. Fallback: the Wachaubahn or the north-bank road, and the ÖBB regional trains between Melk and Krems.

**The bike reservation you need is sold out.** Long-distance ÖBB bike slots are capped and non-flexible. Fallback: chain two regional trains, Passau-Linz-Amstetten runs frequently and takes bikes without reservation.
**A summer Föhn headwind.** The valley can blow hard upstream for a day. Fallback: the itinerary has slack on Day 5 and Day 6; shorten the Göttweig loop rather than compressing the Wachau.

**Accommodation gap in the Wachau.** Between Melk and Krems there are fewer than a dozen villages with rooms, and river-cruise season books them out. Fallback: sleep in Mautern or Rossatz on the south bank, which are quieter and rarely full.
